evidence.claim: The Northwest Passage Scenic Byway is an All-American Road; the Federal Highway Administration’s archived description emphasizes rivers, deep canyons and rugged mountains in Nez Perce country.
evidence.quote: Northwest Passage Scenic Byway All-American Road • Idaho

evidence.claim: the Federal Highway Administration’s archived description emphasizes rivers, deep canyons and rugged mountains in Nez Perce country.
evidence.quote: The sparkling rivers, deep canyons, and rugged mountains they encountered are relatively unchanged. Experience the culture, recreation, and scenery in this breathtaking land of the Nez Perce.

evidence.claim: That description gives six hours for driving the entire 202-mile byway.
evidence.quote: Length 202.0 mi / 325.1 km Time to Allow Six hours to drive or three days to enjoy the entire byway

evidence.claim: The Lolo Trail crossing was already in use by Nez Perce in the eighteenth century, and carried Lewis and Clark west in 1805.
evidence.quote: The trail, known as naptnišaqs, or "Nez Perce Trail" in Salish, was used by Nez Perce in the 18th century, and by the Lewis and Clark Expedition

evidence.claim: The modern highway took decades to complete.
evidence.quote: By late 1955, 27 miles (43 km) remained unfinished, and, upon its completion in 1962, it was redesignated US 12.

evidence.claim: Designated State Highway 9 in 1916, the Lewis and Clark Highway entered construction in 1920.
evidence.quote: The Lewis and Clark Highway, from Lewiston eastward to Lolo Pass, was designated SH-9 in 1916 and construction began in 1920.

evidence.claim: Federal prisoners worked on it in the late 1930s and early 1940s; Japanese internees from Kooskia Internment Camp worked on it during the last two years of World War II.
evidence.quote: Federal prison labor was used in the late 1930s to early 1940s, and Japanese internment labor was used during the last two years of World War II, working out of the Kooskia Internment Camp

evidence.claim: Completion came in 1962, when the road became US 12.
evidence.quote: upon its completion in 1962, it was redesignated US 12.

evidence.claim: Driving east from Lewiston, follow the Clearwater through Orofino and Kamiah, then toward the junction with Idaho 13 across the river from Kooskia.
evidence.quote: Entering Clearwater County, US-12 continues east along the south bank of the Clearwater River through Orofino.

evidence.claim: Near Orofino, the Lewis and Clark expedition exchanged an overland journey for travel by dugout canoe.
evidence.quote: Nearby is the historical "Canoe Camp," where the Lewis and Clark expedition built five new dugout canoes and embarked on October 7, 1805, downstream to the Pacific Ocean.

evidence.claim: At Canoe Camp, five miles downstream from town, the party built five canoes and departed toward the Pacific on October 7, 1805.
evidence.quote: Nearby is the historical "Canoe Camp," where the Lewis and Clark expedition built five new dugout canoes and embarked on October 7, 1805, downstream to the Pacific Ocean.

evidence.claim: At Canoe Camp, five miles downstream from town
evidence.quote: putting in at "Canoe Camp," five miles (8 km) downstream from Orofino

evidence.claim: From Canoe Camp, their downstream journey reached the Columbia Bar and the Pacific Ocean about six weeks later.
evidence.quote: they reached the Columbia Bar and the Pacific Ocean about six weeks later.

evidence.claim: Orofino’s later transport connection ran on rails: the railroad from Lewiston was built in 1899 and later became part of the Camas Prairie Railroad.
evidence.quote: The railroad, later part of the Camas Prairie Railroad, was constructed from Lewiston in 1899.

evidence.claim: The town lies along Orofino Creek and the Clearwater’s north bank.
evidence.quote: along Orofino Creek and the north bank of the Clearwater River.

evidence.claim: For the nimíipuu, or Nez Perce, this landmark near Kamiah is a creation site.
evidence.quote: For the nimíipuu , or Nez Perce, the story of their people begins at the landmark near present day Kamiah, Idaho called timʼné•pe , or Heart of the Monster

evidence.claim: The National Park Service tells of Iceye’ye, coyote, killing a monster that was eating the animals.
evidence.quote: where Iceye'ye (coyote) killed a monster who was eating all of the animals.

evidence.claim: An interpretive shelter presents part of the story through exhibits and audio in Nez Perce and English.
evidence.quote: This site has an interpretive shelter with two exhibits and an audio program. These give you the background information on the role of legends in Nez Perce culture and tell part of the “Coyote and the Monster” legend in Nez Perce and in English.

evidence.claim: A short trail leads to the feature and a semicircle of seats.
evidence.quote: A short trail (approx. 0.2 miles) leads to the “Heart of the Monster” feature and a small semi circle of seating.

evidence.claim: At the semicircle, another audio recording tells the Coyote and the Monster story in English beside the landmark itself.
evidence.quote: Here another audio recording tells the “Coyote and the Monster” legend in English.

evidence.claim: The park asks visitors to honor this spiritual place and leave its rock features undisturbed.
evidence.quote: As visitors to a spiritual place for the Nez Perce, we ask you treat Heart of the Monster with the same respect and honor you would show to any other sacred or religious site. Resist the tempation to approach, climb upon, or deface the rock features.

evidence.claim: A cedar log served as the ceremonial barrier when the highway was dedicated at Lolo Pass in August 1962.
evidence.quote: At the August dedication ceremony at Lolo Pass attended by thousands, the states' governors, Bob Smylie of Idaho and Tim Babcock of Montana, cut through a ceremonial cedar log with a two-man crosscut saw.

evidence.claim: Idaho governor Bob Smylie and Montana governor Tim Babcock cut it with a two-man crosscut saw.
evidence.quote: the states' governors, Bob Smylie of Idaho and Tim Babcock of Montana, cut through a ceremonial cedar log with a two-man crosscut saw.

evidence.claim: The older Lolo Trail also crosses this pass.
evidence.quote: The pass is the highest point of the historic Lolo Trail

evidence.claim: Nez Perce used the trail in the eighteenth century; Old Toby of the Shoshone guided Lewis and Clark along it westward in September 1805.
evidence.quote: was used by Nez Perce in the 18th century, and by the Lewis and Clark Expedition, guided by Old Toby of the Shoshone, on their westward snowbound journey in September 1805.

evidence.claim: The expedition returned the following June.
evidence.quote: After a winter at Fort Clatsop in present-day northwestern Oregon, the Corps of Discovery returned the following June.

evidence.claim: At 5,233 feet, the pass lies on the Idaho–Montana boundary in the Bitterroot Range of the northern Rocky Mountains.
evidence.quote: Lolo Pass, elevation 5,233 feet (1,595 m), is a mountain pass in the western United States, in the Bitterroot Range of the northern Rocky Mountains.  It is on the border between the states of Montana and Idaho

The 202-mile byway and 174.410-mile Idaho US 12 are different scopes. Archived FHWA supplies total byway length and drive time; individual highway pages support the Idaho 13 connection to Grangeville, but do not define its designated byway boundaries.
NPS supplies the cultural account and spelling nimíipuu. Wikipedia gives a fuller creation account; omitted pending a Nez Perce community source.
